chunks: The judge Abu Sa'id al-Khalil ibn Ahmad al-Sajisi told me: Al-Hasan ibn Hamdan narrated to us: Abu Mas'ud Isma'il ibn Masood narrated to us: Yazid (who is ibn Zurai') narrated to us - Sa'id (who is ibn Abi 'Urwah) narrated to us - from Qatadah, from Al-Hasan, that Samarah ibn Jundab and Imran ibn Hussayn discussed, and Samarah narrated that he memorized from the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) two silences: a silence when he said Takbir, and a silence when he finished his recitation before bowing. Then Qatadah mentioned the last silence after finishing the recitation of 'Non-Guided and Not Astray' (Al-Fatiha), meaning that was what Samarah memorized, but Imran ibn Hussayn rejected it. He said: So we wrote to Abu ibn Ka'b about this, and it was in his letter to them or his reply to them that Samarah had indeed memorized correctly.

The compiler of this book (may God increase his honor) said: The Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) only remained silent after the recitation so that the Takbir would not be continuous with the recitation, and so that there would be a break between the recitation and the Takbir. This indicates that he did not say 'Amin' after the Opening of the Book (Al-Fatiha) quietly or loudly, because the one speaking quietly or aloud is not silent. And in that is a strong proof for the Shi'a against their opponents in their saying 'Amin' after the Fatiha. And there is no strength save in God the Sublime the Great.

key_terms.غَيْرِ الْمَغْضُوبِ عَلَيْهِمْ وَلَا الض: The final verse of Al-Fatiha ('Non-Guided and Not Astray')

ai.seo_question: Did the Prophet Muhammad say 'Amin' after reciting Al-Fatiha in prayer?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Khisal highlights the ritual silence (sukut) of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him and his family) between the recitation of Al-Fatiha and the Takbir for Ruku', serving as a key evidence (hujjah) in the Shi'a jurisprudential debate regarding the recitation of 'Amin'. The compiler, Shaykh al-Saduq, utilizes the report of Samarah ibn Jundab and the subsequent verification by Ubayy ibn Ka'b to argue that the Prophet's silence indicates 'Amin' was not recited, either silently or aloud, thereby distinguishing Shi'a prayer practice from other schools. This textual analysis underscores the importance of following the Prophet's precise physical and vocal actions in worship as preserved in early hadith literature.

en.dr-ali-peiravi: 2-116 Judge Abu Sa’id Al-Khalil ibn Ahmad al-Sejezy narrated that Al-Hassan ibn Himdan quoted Abu Masood Isma’il ibn Masood, on the authority of Yazid - Zari’a, on the authority of Sa’id - who is Abi Urubeh, on the authority of Qatadat, on the authority of Al-Hassan, “Samrah ibn Jundab and Imran ibn Hussayn had a discussion with each other. Samrat narrated that he remembered two instances when the Prophet (MGB) remained silent: once after saying the Takbir (God is Great) in prayer and the second time after reciting the Opening Chapter of the Quran (Al-Fatiha ) and before bowing down in prayer.” Qatadat then said that the second instance of the Prophet’s (MGB) silence in what Samurah narrated was after saying ‘Qayr al-Maqzoobe va laz-Zaleen’ (…those whose (portion) is not wrath, and who go not astray) .However, Imran ibn Hussayn rejected this. Then they both wrote a letter in this regard to Abi ibn Ka’ab and asked him about this. Abi ibn Ka’ab replied, “What Samurah has remembered is right.”

The compiler of the book - may God increase his honor - said, “The Prophet (MGB) remained silent for a short while after reciting the verses of the Quran and before saying Allahu Akbar (God is Great) to go into the state of bowing down in prayers so that there is a pause in between them. This means that the Prophet (MGB) neither said Amin (Amen) after reciting the Opening Chapter of the Holy Quran (Al-Fatiha ) quietly or loudly. As remaining silent doesn’t imply saying anything, this is a strong proof for the Shiites who oppose saying Amin (Amen) after reciting the Opening Chapter of the Holy Quran (Al-Fatiha ). And there is no strength save in God the Sublime the Great.”
